          GOOGLE LLC’S RESPONSE AND OBJECTION TO OG&E’S MOTION
                  TO AMEND THE PROCEDURAL SCHEDULE

                  Google LLC (“Google”) objects to Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company’s (“OG&E”)

         September 22, 2026 Motion to Amend the Procedural Schedule in Order No. 758969 to Include a

         Briefing Schedule Regarding Proposals for Alternative Electric Service Frameworks (“Motion,”

         Entry No. 45). Google asks that the Motion be denied and that the schedule adopted in Order No.

         758969 remain in place. Google does not object to the Commission hearing legal argument on

         questions properly presented by the evidence. It objects to making a four-round, stand-alone

         briefing sequence a prerequisite to the merits hearing and postponing that hearing until January

         2027.


             I.        The requested amendment would materially delay the merits hearing.

                  1.     Order No. 758969 adopted the parties’ agreed schedule and set the hearing before

         the Commission en banc for November 3, 2026. It provides for OG&E’s rebuttal testimony on

         October 5, sur-rebuttal testimony on October 20, pretrial motions and witness-related filings on

         October 27, and proposed findings and conclusions on November 20. Order No. 758969, at 1–2,

         5 (Entry No. 20).

                  2.    OG&E would retain the testimony deadlines but add briefs-in-chief on October 30,

         responses on November 20, replies on December 4, and sur-replies on December 18. It would

         move pretrial filings to December 29, the en banc merits hearing to January 12, 2027, and proposed

         findings and conclusions to January 29. Motion ¶ 10. Calling that a “slight delay” does not change

         its effect. OG&E asks the Commission to postpone the commencement of the merits hearing by

         more than two months and to move the post-hearing submissions into the following year. Motion

         ¶ 11.


                  II.    OG&E has not shown why the identified legal questions require
                                           postponement.

                  3.    OG&E says that the proposals it labels as “Delivery Only Deregulated Generation

         Election” or “DODGE” raise questions about Commission authority, certified territories, retail

         competition, and electric-service obligations. Motion ¶¶ 4–7. Google does not ask the

         Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”) to resolve those questions through this scheduling motion. Nor

         does Google concede that OG&E’s label accurately describes Google’s proposal. The existence of

         disputed questions of law does not, by itself, establish that the Commission cannot hear the

         evidence and resolve the law on the schedule it has adopted.

                  4.    Order No. 758969 already supplies means to develop the record and address

         focused disputes: rebuttal and sur-rebuttal testimony, defined pretrial motion practice before the

         ALJ, examination at the en banc hearing, and post-hearing proposed findings and conclusions. Id.

         at 2–5. OG&E identifies no specific evidence it is unable to present through those means, no

         particular issue it cannot bring to the ALJ before hearing, and no reason a legal position cannot be

         presented in argument and proposed conclusions on the existing schedule. Its generalized appeals

         to fairness and judicial economy do not explain why four sequential rounds of briefing must

         conclude before any merits hearing begins. Motion ¶¶ 6–10.

                  5.     The proposed sequence is not narrowly tailored to the asserted need. It assigns

         October 30 for briefs-in-chief but gives responding parties until November 20—the date already

         set for proposed findings under the existing order—and carries additional briefs through December

         18. Motion ¶ 10. The Commission should not defer an already scheduled en banc hearing to

         accommodate this structure where OG&E has not shown why ordinary hearing procedures are

         inadequate.


                       III.   The related proceedings do not justify resetting this case.

                  6.     OG&E itself identifies the related large-load issues in Public Service Company of

         Oklahoma’s Case No. PUD2025-000075 and states that similar proposals arose there after the

         parties negotiated the schedule in this case. Motion ¶ 3 & n.1. Google does not contend that the

         cases present identical records or that an ALJ recommendation or proposed stipulation in another

         docket binds this Commission here. But the existence of a related proceeding is not a reason to

         prevent the Commission from hearing the proposals and objections on this record on November 3.

         OG&E’s claim that formal legal briefing did not occur in the other proceeding does not establish

         that a four-round briefing process is indispensable here. Google requests separate, timely

         consideration of each case on its own record.

                  7.     OG&E has also itself sought prompt Commission action on large-load-related

         arrangements in Case No. PUD2026-000031. Its application there concerns electric service

         agreements with a Google affiliate for significant new load, describes tariff-based pricing and

         possible migration to a future Commission-approved large-load tariff, and requests an order by

         October 31, 2026. Application, Case No. PUD2026-000031, at 1–4 (Entry No. 1). That special-

         contract and capacity-purchase application does not decide the legality of the self-supply proposal

         in this case. It does demonstrate that large-load service and the timing of Commission action are

         significant to OG&E as well as to the other parties. Google does not seek to import the merits of

         that separate application into this tariff case.


             IV.       The effect of the requested postponement warrants particular scrutiny.

                  8.      The current order calls for the en banc hearing to commence November 3, 2026.

         OG&E would instead commence it January 12, 2027. Publicly stated term dates indicate that

         Commissioner J. Todd Hiett’s term ends January 11, 2027, and that the next term begins that day.

         Thus OG&E’s requested schedule would move the opening of the merits hearing across a

         scheduled change in Commission membership. Google does not ask the ALJ to find, without

         evidence, that OG&E chose these dates to secure a particular Commissioner or outcome. The

         objective consequence nonetheless reinforces the need for a concrete explanation of why

         postponement is necessary. The Motion supplies none.

                  9.      The Commission can evaluate the proposed tariff, Google’s alternative, and

         OG&E’s statutory objections on a developed record without prejudging any of them. To the extent

         an asserted legal defect turns on the terms of a future customer arrangement not yet before the

         Commission, the parties can identify the precise issue and the Commission can determine what, if

         anything, should be resolved now. Neither hypothetical implementation disputes nor disagreement

         with responsive testimony warrants delaying the entire tariff hearing.

                                            V.      Requested relief

                  10.   Google requests that the ALJ deny OG&E’s Motion, decline to recommend any

         amendment to Order No. 758969, and preserve the November 3, 2026 en banc hearing and all

         associated deadlines. Google further requests such other relief as is just and appropriate without

         amending the existing procedural schedule. Google reserves its position on the merits of OG&E’s

         legal objections and on any separate motion concerning testimony.
